'''''Ficus coronata''''', commonly known as the '''sandpaper fig''' or '''creek sandpaper fig''', is a [[Cauliflory|cauliflorous]] species of [[ficus|fig]] tree, native to [[Australia]]. It is found along the east coast from [[Mackay, Queensland|Mackay]] in [[Central Queensland]], through [[New South Wales]] and just into [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] near [[Mallacoota]]. It grows along river banks and gullies in rainforest and open forest. Its common name is derived from its rough sandpapery leaves, which it shares with the other [[sandpaper fig]]s.

==Taxonomy==
''Ficus coronata'' was first described by the Italian Marquese di Spigno in 1818. Its [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] the [[Latin]] ''coronata'' "crowned", referring to a ring of bristles around the apex of the fruit. ''Ficus stephanocarpa'' (also meaning 'crowned fruit') as described by the German botanist [[Otto Warburg (botanist)|Otto Warburg]]  is a synonym.<ref name=EJ15>{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W |author2=Jones, David L |author3=Blake, Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Volume 4 (Eu-Go)|year=1986|pages=213–X |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-589-9}}</ref>

==Description==
The sandpaper fig is a small tree which may reach the dimensions of {{convert|6|–|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|3|–|5|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide, although is generally smaller. The trunk is dark brown, and the ovate or elliptical leaves are {{convert|5|–|15|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|2|–|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide and very scabrous (rough) like [[sandpaper]] on the upper side. The new growth is hairy. The succulent oval fruit is around {{convert|1.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and covered in dense hairs.<ref name=EJ15/><ref name=Fairley>{{cite book|author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |pages=61–62|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The sandpaper fig is found along watercourses and gullies in rainforest, and less commonly in open forest. It may be associated with the rough-barked apple (''[[Angophora floribunda]]'').<ref name=Ben98>{{cite journal|last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1998 |title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=809–987 |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf |accessdate=2008-02-19 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071007171819/http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf |archivedate=2007-10-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is found on limestone outcrops in [[Kanangra-Boyd National Park]].<ref name=DEC>{{cite web|url=http://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/resources/protectedareas/kowmungwra08366.pdf|title=Kowmung River, Kanangra-Boyd National Park: Wild River Assessment|last=Parks and Wildlife Division |date=2005|publisher=Department of Environment and Conservation (NSW)|accessdate=23 April 2012}}</ref> It is found from [[Mackay, Queensland|Mackay]] southwards through New South Wales and into eastern Victoria where it is listed as "threatened" under the [[Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988]].<ref name=TL>{{cite web | title=Threatened List March 2008 | work = Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988 | date = 10 November 2020 | publisher = Department of Sustainability and Environment|url = http://www.dse.vic.gov.au/CA256F310024B628/0/36B3DDD055E821CCCA2574960015839C/$File/FFG+threatened+list+March+2008.pdf}}</ref>

A study showed the species has recently expanded into south eastern New South Wales and into Victoria.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wilde |first1=Brendan C. |last2=Rutherford |first2=Susan |last3=Yap |first3=Jia-Yee S. |last4=Rossetto |first4=Maurizio |date=June 2021 |title=Allele Surfing and Holocene Expansion of an Australian Fig (Ficus—Moraceae) |journal=Diversity |language=en |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=250 |doi=10.3390/d13060250 |bibcode=2021Diver..13..250W |issn=1424-2818|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Ficus coronata'' serves as a food plant for the caterpillars of the Queensland butterflies, the common- or purple moonbeam (''[[Philiris innotatus]]'')<ref>{{cite book |title=The Complete Field Guide to Butterflies of Australia |url=https://archive.org/details/The_Complete_Field_Guide_to_Butterflies_of_Australia |last=Braby |first=Michael F.|year=2005 |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |location=Collingwood, Victoria |isbn=0-643-09027-4 |page=[https://archive.org/details/The_Complete_Field_Guide_to_Butterflies_of_Australia/page/n237 228]}}</ref> and the common crow (''[[Euploea core]]'').<ref>{{Cite web |title=SOWN (Save Our Waterways Now) |url=https://sown.com.au/ficus-coronata-moraceae-creek-sandpaper-fig/ |access-date=29 November 2023 |website=Ficus coronata (MORACEAE) Creek Sandpaper Fig|date=8 June 2020 }}</ref> The [[Australasian figbird]] (''Sphecotheres vieilloti''), [[green catbird]] (''Ailuroedus crassirostris''), [[olive-backed oriole]] (''Oriolus sagittatus''), [[topknot pigeon]] (''Lopholaimus antarcticus''), and [[grey-headed flying fox]] (''Pteropus poliocephalus'') are among those animals who consume the fruit.<ref name="Floyd09">{{cite book|last=Floyd|first=Alex G.|title=Rainforest Trees of Mainland Southeastern Australia|publisher=Terania Rainforest Publishing|location=Lismore, NSW|year=2009|page=230|isbn=978-0-9589436-7-3}}</ref>

==Uses==
The fruit is edible and palatable,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lindsay |first=Lenore|date=March 1992 |title=Fancy a feast? Try a fig. |journal=Australian Plants |volume=16 |issue=130 |pages=251–52}}</ref> and was consumed by local Aboriginal people.

A popular story holds that the fig's leaves were used as sandpaper for polishing wood or turtle shells by indigenous people. Bonsai and fig enthusiast Len Webber stated they were too brittle and soft to function in this fashion,<ref>{{cite book |title=Rainforest to Bonsai |last=Webber |first=Len |year=1991 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |location=East Roseville, NSW |isbn=0-7318-0237-3 |page=125}}</ref> but a more recent example found they did work.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.thefigsofaustralia.com/ficus-coronata-leaves-as-sandpaper/|title=Ficus coronata leaves as sandpaper|date=3 July 2020}}</ref>

The sandpaper fig's leaves are an attractive attribute which may be highlighted with [[bonsai]], although the trunk may not thicken spontaneously.<ref>{{cite book |title=Bonsai with Australian native Plants |author=Koreshoff, Dorothy and Vita |year=1984 |publisher=Boolarong Publications |location=Brisbane |isbn=0-908175-66-3 |page=52}}</ref> It is suited to a shady position in gardens, or medium to brightly lit indoor spaces.<ref>{{cite book |title=Australian Native Plants for Indoors |last=Ratcliffe |first=David & Patricia|year=1987 |publisher=Little Hills Press |location=Crows Nest, NSW |isbn=0-949773-49-2 |page=89}}</ref> Like all figs in garden situations, they attract birds,<ref>{{cite book |title=Attracting Wildlife to Your Garden |last=Elliot |first=Rodger |authorlink=Rodger Elliot |year=1994 |publisher=Lothian Books |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-628-3 |page=58}}</ref> such as species of [[Zosterops|silvereye]] and rainforest pigeon.<ref>{{cite book |title=Attracting Birds to Your Garden |last=Dengate |first=John |year=1994 |publisher=New Holland Press |location=Kenthurst |isbn=1-86436-411-4 |page=23}}</ref>
